title: Nova Scotian’s NHL debut didn’t feel real until he got punched in the face, he says
summary: Dillon Boucher, who grew up in Head of Chezzetcook, made his NHL debut with the Chicago Blackhawks last week at the age of 29 after grinding it out in the minor leagues for several seasons.

image.caption: Dillon Boucher of Head of Chezzetcook, N.S. is escorted off the ice by a linesman after fighting Tampa Bay Lightning forward Jeffrey Viel in his second NHL game on November 05, 2026. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Dillon Boucher, who grew up in Head of Chezzetcook, made his NHL debut with the Chicago Blackhawks last week at the age of 29 after grinding it out in the minor leagues for several seasons.
Head of Chezzetcook’s Dillon Boucher, 29, played first NHL game with Chicago Blackhawks last week
It took Nova Scotia’s Dillon Boucher getting into a fight for it to sink in that he was finally playing in the National Hockey League.
“People are like, ‘When did it feel real?’ I think when I got punched in the face a few times,” he told CBC News from his apartment in Chicago.
Boucher, who grew up in Head of Chezzetcook N.S., made his NHL debut with the Chicago Blackhawks last week at the age of 29 after grinding it out in the minor leagues for several seasons.
In his second game, he dropped the gloves with Tampa Bay Lightning forward Jeremy Viel.
It was a good tilt, says Boucher, who is still sporting a black eye and a cut on his forehead.
“Might not be able to get any modeling debut right now but, no, it was fun,” he said.
Boucher, who is known more for his physical play and hockey IQ than for scoring goals, admits he wasn’t sure if he’d ever get this opportunity.
But now that he is he says he’s working hard to make the most of it while trying to enjoy every moment along the way.
“I know nothing's guaranteed. I kind of take it day by day. I've never been one to look too far in the future or look too far in the past,” Boucher said.
He was mature then and he’s mature now
Boucher's mindset is no surprise to one of his former minor hockey coaches.
“He was a mature young man then. He's a mature young man now,” said Paddy Flynn, director of hockey at Mount Academy, a private university in North Rustico, P.E.I.
Flynn coached Boucher several years ago on a major bantam team in Nova Scotia. He immediately noticed the young player had a lot of skills that aren’t necessarily celebrated in the sport, he says.

Dillon Boucher says he was able to continue to pursue his dream of playing in the NHL because of the support he's received from his family and friends. In this photo (from left to right) he's with his brother Justin, mother Colette and father Brad. (Courtesy of Colette Boucher)

“It was obvious that he had a high hockey IQ, cerebral player [and] very defensive minded. I think, you know, he was taught that at an early age and I think that it's carried through to where he's at now,” Flynn said.
Since Boucher was already skilled on the ice, Flynn believes he had more of an influence on the player away from the rink.
The two had many conversations that were more about life than hockey, the coach said.

Dillon Boucher played for the Cape Breton Screaming Eagles and Charlottetown Islanders of the QMJHL. He also suited up for Dalhousie University before stints in the ECHL and AHL. (Cape Breton Screaming Eagles/Facebook)
Flynn, who also coaches the U18 men’s team at Mount Academy, admits he got emotional watching Boucher take the ice for the first time in a Chicago Blackhawks jersey.
He watched the game with several young players from the academy and he feels Boucher's story inspired them.
“I believe that it would have resonated with a number of them for sure,” Flynn said.
“The hard work and the commitment to getting there. There's the message. He made it.”
